Frame Assassination.short_definition: Answering a concern about something someone did by swapping the whole topic for the other person's character or emotional state.
Frame Assassination.expanded_definition: You raise something specific: 'You cancelled on me three times this month.' The reply does not dispute it or defend it. It swaps the subject: 'Why are you so angry all the time?' Your original point has not been refused, which is why it is hard to notice that it was never answered. One topic change in a tense talk is ordinary. The pattern is when each attempt to return to your point is sent back to the new topic, and the conversation ends up being about you.
Frame Assassination.plain_language_summary: You bring up something someone did, and the conversation turns into a discussion of what is wrong with you, so your original point never gets answered.
Frame Assassination.why_this_matters: You arrive with a concern about an action and leave defending your own stability. Your point was never refused, so it is hard to notice that it was never answered, and harder to explain to anyone else why you feel unheard.
what_it_is: A switch of subject from what was done to who the speaker says you are, such as 'this is about your temper, not my schedule.'
More complete than drifting: the old topic is declared closed or renamed, and a new one is put in its place.
Usually set off by a concrete complaint, and aimed at your mood, your tone, your history or your motives.
Persistent: restating your original point gets it sent back to the new frame.
Can happen in writing too, where a reply to a list of grievances addresses only how the list was worded.
what_it_sounds_like: This isn't about the dishes. This is about how unstable you've been lately.
I'm not going to discuss that until you calm down and look at why you're like this.
Do you hear yourself? That's the real issue here.
We're not talking about what I said, we're talking about the way you took it.
You always do this: you find something to be upset about and make it everyone's problem.
Your email asks about the missed payment; the reply is two paragraphs on how hostile your tone was, and nothing on the payment.
I think what you need to ask yourself is why this bothers you so much.
what_it_is_not: Conversations drift, and steering one back together is ordinary; someone can also raise a real worry about your wellbeing without meaning to displace what you said. The test is whether the original topic can be returned to at all.
Agreeing to pause a heated talk and come back when both are calmer, with a time named and kept.
Adding a second issue alongside yours, such as 'I want to hear that, and I also felt hurt last week.'
A reply that disputes the facts of your complaint, which is disagreement and not a change of subject.
A mediator or counselor widening the lens to the whole relationship, with both people's agreement.
Someone going straight to their feelings because they heard your complaint as a verdict on them, then coming back to your point.
this_may_be_it_when: Your complaint names an action and the reply names a trait.
You can state your point three times and each time end up back at the new topic.
The conversation ends with you apologizing for how you raised it.
The new topic is one you did not start and cannot easily refuse, such as your tone or mood.
Days later, the original issue has no answer and nobody has mentioned it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your original point gets an answer, even a disagreeing one, before anything else is raised.
They ask 'can I say how this feels to me first?' and then return to your issue.
The concern they raise about you is specific, such as that you have been sleeping badly, and they stay on your topic too.
A time to resume is named and kept.
You yourself realize your original complaint was really about something else.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people go straight to feelings when they feel attacked, and hear a complaint as a verdict on them.
In a long, tense talk both people lose the thread, and the topic changes without anyone choosing it.
A person anxious about conflict may grab a different subject to lower the temperature.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'let's park this, I'm too tired to do it justice' and brings it back the next day.
A counselor who asks what else is going on for you, as part of an agreed session.
A partner who answers your complaint and also adds their own, so two topics now share the table.
discernment_questions: Can I still find my original point anywhere in this conversation?
When I restate it, does it get answered, or is it sent back to the new topic?
Is the new subject something they would also raise on a calm day, with no complaint from me?
Do I leave these talks defending myself about things I never meant to discuss?
Would someone listening in say my concern was ever answered?
less_concerning_if: Your point gets at least a short answer before the talk widens.
The subject changes only when both of you are worn out, and returns when you are rested.
They can say afterward what your original concern was.
more_concerning_if: The substitute topic is always your character, mood or mental state.
You have stopped raising concerns because you know how they will end.
Other people are told the argument was about your reaction, not about the thing that set it off.
pattern_over_time_signs: You open complaints with long disclaimers about your tone, hoping to prevent the swap.
You find old concerns unanswered, with no memory of them being settled.
You say 'never mind' to end the talk, though the issue is unchanged.
Over months you bring up fewer concerns, and the list you keep in your head gets longer.
Frame Assassination.repair_check: Once you point out the swap, a changed exchange looks like them stating your original point back to you and answering it, even if the answer is no. An apology about the argument that never touches the original issue leaves that issue where it was.
Frame Assassination.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether you can hold your topic. Say once, 'I'd like an answer to my first question,' and see if it gets one. If the reply is more about you, the request was met with the very move it was about.
Frame Assassination.psychological_mechanism: People tend to follow whichever topic is emotionally louder. A remark about your character or stability is hard to ignore, so attention moves to defending yourself, which is more tiring than complaining. Because the new frame is personal, correcting it can feel like proving the point, and the original concern gets quietly dropped by the person who raised it.
Frame Assassination.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving a talk unable to say what they had meant to ask, replaying it for hours, and wondering whether they really are as difficult as they were just told. Some begin rehearsing complaints in advance, or stop raising them. A slow sense that nothing they bring up ever gets settled is also common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the swap and ask for both topics: 'I'd like to hear how I come across, and I'd also like an answer to what I first asked. Can we do mine first?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your topic: 'That may be worth talking about, but it's not the subject today. I asked about the cancelled plans.'
response_options.disengagement: If the new topic keeps winning, stop the exchange and put the original concern in a short written note you can point back to.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend your original question and ask them to say back what they hear. If they can state it clearly, you know the question was not the problem.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put the concern in an email naming the action and the date, and ask for a reply on that point. A written thread keeps the topic from drifting.

Frame Assassination.boundary_script: "I notice we've moved from what I asked to how I'm asking. Could you tell me in one sentence what you make of the cancelled plans? Then I'll gladly hear what's on your mind."
Frame Assassination.safety_note: On its own this is a conversation problem, not a danger sign. The picture changes if raising a concern starts to bring threats, punishments, or talk of your mental state to doctors or relatives. If that happens, note what was said and when, and talk to a counselor or advocate you trust before the next conversation about it.
misuse_warning: Calling it frame killing whenever a talk changes topic punishes ordinary drift and hides the times you changed the subject yourself.
Used as an accusation, 'you're killing my frame' can itself replace the other person's concern, which is the move it describes.
Frame Assassination.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Priming installs a lens before a talk; Frame Assassination removes yours during one. Projection returns your complaint as an accusation of the same behavior, while this tactic returns it as a remark about you. Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown answers with a psychological-sounding term such as 'that's your trauma', where Frame Assassination can use any substitute at all: your tone, your mood, your history.
Frame Assassination.core_meaning: Answering a concern about something someone did by swapping the whole topic for the other person's character or emotional state.

Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.short_definition: Describing a person's boundaries, reactions or differences as symptoms of a disorder, so that protecting themselves reads as proof something is wrong with them.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.expanded_definition: Ordinary responses get reread in clinical vocabulary: saying no is 'avoidant', being upset is 'a meltdown', needing space is 'a symptom'. The terms sound informed, but they come from people who are not assessing you and are used against what you just said. A trusted person can name a real change out of concern. This pattern is where each limit you set is answered with a label, so the next limit costs more to set.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.plain_language_summary: When you set a limit or react strongly, you are told it is a symptom, so protecting yourself starts to look like proof that something is wrong with you.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.why_this_matters: Self-protection gets reclassified as a symptom, so your boundaries cost you credibility and any pushback is read as further evidence of the alleged problem. You may stop setting limits at all, since each one can be turned into proof.
what_it_is: A word from the mental-health vocabulary attached to a response, such as 'paranoid' for asking where someone was.
Applied to limits and reactions that would be reasonable for most people in the same situation.
Self-sealing: objecting to the label is taken as more of the symptom.
May be said in front of others or written into messages and notes, which lets it travel.
Different from a diagnosis given by a clinician after assessment; here nobody has assessed anything.
what_it_sounds_like: That's just your anxiety talking.
You're being paranoid. Normal people don't ask that.
You're so avoidant. This is why you can't keep relationships.
I think you're having an episode.
Maybe you should get that checked, because it's not normal to react like this.
A group chat describes your request for quiet as 'one of her moods.'
A message to your family says you have 'been struggling with your mental health' right after you declined a request.
what_it_is_not: A trusted person can gently name a real escalation out of care, and a diagnosis someone has disclosed themselves can be referred to supportively. What is described here is a boundary answered with a label instead of a response.
A clinician who has assessed you explaining a diagnosis you asked about.
Someone using these words about themselves: 'I'm anxious about this, can we slow down?'
A friend saying 'you don't seem like yourself lately,' then asking about it and listening.
Calling for help when someone seems truly unsafe, which is a response to a crisis and not a rebuttal of a limit.
this_may_be_it_when: Your limit is answered with a term about you, not with a reply to the limit.
The person using the term has never assessed you and is not qualified to.
The label comes up each time you say no and rarely at other times.
Reasonable people in your position would have said the same.
The label is shared with others as an explanation for why you cannot be taken seriously.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You have a diagnosis you chose to share, and they refer to it respectfully and still honor the limit.
The concern is about a clear change in you, like not eating, and is raised privately and with care.
The term is used by someone qualified, in a session you chose to attend.
Your limit is respected first, and concern is raised separately.
They are describing their own state, not yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Mental-health words are now everyday speech, and people use them loosely with no plan to dismiss anyone.
A person may truly be worried and not know another way to put it.
People who struggle themselves may see their own struggles in others.
common_false_positives: A sibling who notices you have not been sleeping and asks whether you are all right.
A counselor naming a pattern you have both agreed to examine.
A friend who says 'I think I'm getting anxious, can we slow down?', talking about themselves.
discernment_questions: Would most people in my position react as I did?
Does the label show up when I set a limit and not otherwise?
Do they have any training or basis for the term, and have they ever asked about my life?
Do they say the label to others about me?
Can I disagree with the label without it being taken as more evidence?
less_concerning_if: The term is raised once, privately, and dropped when you answer.
Your limit is respected whatever is said.
They apply the same words to themselves.
more_concerning_if: The label is shared with family, coworkers or officials.
Your reaction to being labeled is cited as proof of it.
Decisions about you, such as who has a say in your care, your home or your children, begin to refer to the label.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop stating limits, because stating them has begun to cost more than it protects.
You start using their words on yourself, asking 'am I just being anxious?' before you speak.
People around you begin to repeat the term.
You are seen as 'the one with issues' by people who never saw what led up to each reaction.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.repair_check: Repair would be the limit being respected first, then the label withdrawn in front of whoever heard it. Someone apologizing for 'how it came out' while still holding that you have a problem has changed the tone but not the claim.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.boundary_respect_check: State a limit and see whether the answer is about the limit or about you. 'Okay, I won't ask for that' answers the limit. Any reply that includes a word for your mental state sends the limit back unanswered.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.psychological_mechanism: Clinical words carry authority, and few people feel qualified to argue with them. When your response is renamed as a symptom, defending it can feel like confirming it. Being told something is wrong with you again and again can lead you to weigh your own reactions less and the other person's reading more, and others may come to treat your boundaries as optional.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe second-guessing normal reactions, apologizing for needing space, and hiding upset so as not to supply evidence. Some look up the terms used about them or ask others whether they are 'too much'. Some describe grief or anger at having been misread for years.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask what they are basing the term on: 'Is there something specific I did that worries you? I'd rather talk about that than a label.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate your limit from your health: 'My answer is about the request, not about my mental health. I'm asking you to respect that.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not argue your sanity point by point. Ask for a pause of a few hours or a day, then return to the request in writing.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted friend, or a clinician of your own choosing, which words are being used about you, and ask whether they match what they see. An outside view helps you check.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a label is used about you at work, school or in a care setting, ask in writing what it is based on and who has seen it, and take it to HR, a union representative or an advocate.

Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.boundary_script: "I understand you're worried, and I'd like to talk about what actually happened. When you call my answer a symptom, I can't respond to that. What I said was no to this request. Can we stay with the request?"
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.safety_note: Watch for the label being used outside the conversation: shared with family, an employer, a school, a doctor or a court, or used to explain why your account should not count. Also watch for talk of treatment you did not ask for. Keep dated copies of messages, and speak to a legal aid service or an advocate before any meeting where the label may come up.
misuse_warning: Not every mention of mental health about someone is pathologizing. Treating all concern as an attack can leave a person alone when they are struggling.
Applying this label to someone who is sincerely worried about you can turn a hard moment into a rupture. Check whether your limit was actually answered.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Invalidation tells you your feeling is not valid; pathologizing names a disorder that supposedly explains it. Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis uses a diagnosis to close one particular complaint, while this keeps going across your everyday limits and reactions. Authority Hijack tells you what you really feel; this tells you which condition you have.
Identity Diminishment via Pathologizing.core_meaning: Describing a person's boundaries, reactions or differences as symptoms of a disorder, so that protecting themselves reads as proof something is wrong with them.

Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.short_definition: Using therapy-sounding phrases such as 'you're projecting' or 'that's your trauma' as the whole answer to a concrete complaint, so the talk ends.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.expanded_definition: Phrases borrowed from therapy, such as 'you're projecting', 'this is your trauma' or 'you're triggered', can offer real insight in the right place. Used as the entire reply to something specific, like 'you didn't pay the bill', they move the problem inside you, where nobody can check it. A claim about your inner life can be neither proven nor disproven, so it can't be answered, and the talk stops. One use proves little; the pattern is the same few phrases appearing whatever you raise.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.plain_language_summary: A concrete complaint gets met with a therapy-sounding phrase like 'you're projecting', and the conversation ends without anything being addressed.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.why_this_matters: A specific, checkable complaint is converted into something untestable about your inner life, which closes the conversation without anything being resolved or even disputed. You leave with the problem unsolved and a new doubt about yourself.
what_it_is: A short psychological phrase offered as a full answer: 'you're projecting.'
Borrowed from therapy, where such ideas are explored with consent and in good faith, and used here to end an exchange.
Hard to answer because it claims something about your inner life that nobody can check.
The same few phrases return, whatever you bring up.
Different from an observation that arrives alongside real engagement with your point.
what_it_sounds_like: You're projecting.
That's your trauma talking, not me.
You're just triggered right now.
This is clearly about your father, not about what I did.
You have attachment issues, and that's what this is.
I can't have a conversation with someone who's dysregulated.
Your email about the missing invoice is answered with 'I think you have some things to unpack.'
what_it_is_not: 'You're projecting' is sometimes accurate, and in a therapy room that kind of exploration is the agreed purpose of being there. The marker is a psychological reading offered as the whole reply to a concrete complaint.
A pause to settle down ('I'm too upset to talk well, can we come back at six?') that is followed by a return.
Someone describing their own triggers: 'That topic is hard for me because of my past.'
A real observation offered together with an answer to your complaint.
A therapist's or friend's interpretation that you asked for.
Shared therapy vocabulary in a household where both of you use it lightly and mean it.
this_may_be_it_when: The phrase comes as the entire reply, with nothing about the matter itself.
The same handful of terms answers different complaints.
The complaint concerns something checkable, like money, dates or a promise.
You did not ask for an interpretation.
The talk ends and nothing changes.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The reading comes with an answer on the complaint.
You asked for their view on your patterns.
It is said in a therapy session where interpretation is the task.
They use the same words about themselves with equal readiness.
The talk continues after the phrase.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Therapy vocabulary has become everyday speech, and many people use it with no wish to end the talk.
When flooded with feeling, someone may grasp at a word that feels like understanding.
People who have been helped by therapy sometimes apply its lens to everything, sincerely.
common_false_positives: A friend noting 'I think this is about your last job' while still discussing your complaint.
A partner in couples counseling naming a pattern the counselor suggested.
Someone saying 'I'm triggered, I need an hour' about themselves, and returning after the hour.
discernment_questions: Is my concrete point answered, or only my psychology?
Would the same phrase be used for any complaint I made?
Could the claim be tested, and does anyone want to test it?
Did I ever ask them for an interpretation of my feelings?
After the phrase, did the topic return?
less_concerning_if: The phrase is followed by a real answer.
You asked for their psychological view and wanted to hear it.
They accept that it cannot settle the facts.
more_concerning_if: The same phrases end every disagreement.
Others hear that you are 'triggered' or 'projecting' before they hear your complaint.
Practical matters like money, promises or safety stay unaddressed because of it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start prefacing every complaint with a disclaimer such as 'I know this might be my stuff'.
Disputes end in the same two or three phrases.
You read about psychology to check whether you are really doing what you are told.
Issues you raised months ago are still unanswered, as though they were resolved.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.repair_check: Repair is the original complaint finally getting a reply, even a disagreeing one, and the therapy words dropping out of disputes. A sincere-sounding 'maybe I shouldn't use those words' followed by the same words next time is a change in apology only.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.boundary_respect_check: Watch the reply that follows a request to stick to the facts. A reply that takes up the facts, even to disagree, has taken the request. A fresh psychological term has not.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.psychological_mechanism: Psychological language carries an air of expertise, and few people feel confident enough to dispute it on the spot. Because 'you're projecting' cannot be proven or disproven, the only way to answer it is to defend your inner life, which pulls the talk away from the facts. Repeated, it can teach you to examine yourself before examining the complaint.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a specific frustration: leaving a talk with the problem untouched and a new worry that they might be the problem. Some start reading about psychology to rule themselves out, or stop bringing up issues at all. Others say it felt like being politely told they were not worth answering.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer to consider it later, and ask for the reply now: 'Maybe, and I'm happy to look at that. First, did the payment go through?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what the talk is about: 'I'm asking about the payment. Please answer that.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop the exchange when a term replaces an answer, and put the concrete question in writing so that it stands on the page.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the whole exchange to someone you trust, including the original complaint, and ask: was my question answered? Hearing yourself summarize it often makes this clear.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, restate the issue as a business matter in an email with a date and a request for a reply, and keep the thread.

Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.boundary_script: "You may be right that my past plays a part, and I'm open to talking about that another time. This conversation is about the invoice. Can you tell me when it will be paid?"
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.safety_note: Mostly a conversation problem. It becomes a safety matter if the phrases are used to explain away threats, injuries or money taken, or if you are told you are too unwell to be believed by others. If so, record specific events with dates and talk to an advocate or counselor outside the relationship.
misuse_warning: Saying 'that's just therapy-speak' to dismiss every psychological observation can shut out a useful one. Ask whether your point was also answered.
Using 'that's pseudo-insight' as a comeback is itself a psychology-sounding reply that avoids the point.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Projection is a specific accusation returned to you; Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown is an interpretation of you that needs nothing from your complaint. Emotional Invalidation tells you your feeling is too much, while this one sets the feeling aside and offers a theory of where it comes from. Frame Assassination swaps the topic to your character or mood, where this one names a psychological mechanism and stops.
Pseudo-Insight as Shutdown.core_meaning: Using therapy-sounding phrases such as 'you're projecting' or 'that's your trauma' as the whole answer to a concrete complaint, so the talk ends.
